motion: On balance, is religion a force for good in the world?

pro.label: Religion is a force for good

con.label: Religion is not a force for good

lockedRoutes.description: Establish that religion, considered on balance, generates substantial humanitarian, moral, spiritual, and reconciliatory goods despite acknowledged religious harms.
lockedRoutes.successCriteria: Show that religious faith distinctively motivates significant good, that its harmful forms are not exhaustive or essential, and that constructive religious practice can outweigh or materially answer the cited harms.

motionBridge.description: Religion is, on balance, a force for good in the world.

centralBridges.description: Religious belief supplies a distinctive and widespread motivation for charity, forgiveness, service, and moral self-discipline.
Religious wrongdoing is a perversion or contingent misuse of faith rather than an exhaustive measure of religion's effects.
Pluralistic and interfaith religious practice can help reconcile divided communities and support peaceful coexistence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Belief in a higher power can foster humility, obligation, purpose, and spiritual enrichment.
Fanaticism, prejudice, and violence also arise from secular political, ethnic, and ideological sources.

lockedRoutes.description: Establish that religion's supernatural authority, institutional doctrines, and exclusivist identities impose grave harms while its alleged goods remain available through secular human capacities.
lockedRoutes.successCriteria: Show that religion adds unnecessary epistemic submission and divisive authority to ordinary human morality, produces serious characteristic harms, and cannot claim distinctive credit for goods achievable without it.

motionBridge.description: Religion is not, on balance, a force for good in the world.

centralBridges.description: Religion requires surrender to unsupported supernatural and human religious authority at the cost of intellectual and moral freedom.
Religious doctrine and identity intensify violence, exclusion, sexual oppression, and resistance to medicine or evidence.
Moral knowledge, charity, solidarity, and transcendent experience do not require religion, so religious institutions cannot claim unique credit for them.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Covenantal and one-true-faith claims multiply existing ethnic and political divisions.
Concrete cases such as clerical AIDS policy, Northern Ireland, Rwanda, and sectarian conflict test claims that religion is benign.

lockedSections.title: Humanitarian work, attributable good, and countervailing harm
lockedSections.rationale: The central comparative dispute is whether large-scale faith-based service demonstrates religion's positive balance or whether such service is non-distinctive and outweighed by doctrinal harms.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Faith-based organizations provide extensive health care and relief, while the shared ethical essence of major faiths motivates compassion and service, making the claim that religion is unadulterated poison unsustainable.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Almost half of health care in Africa is delivered by faith-based organizations... It can also create a deep well of compassion... stimulating the impulse to do good, disciplining the propensity to be selfish and bad.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: Religious charity does not establish a positive balance because religious doctrine can help cause the conditions being relieved, harmful organizations also perform charity, and ordinary moral concern requires no divine source.

sourceSpan.excerpt: we'd be told about charity... Name me one religion that stands for that... AIDS was not as bad as condoms... Hamas and Hezbollah... do a great deal of charitable work. It's nothing compared to the harm that they do.

lockedSections.title: Religious motivation versus secular moral sufficiency
lockedSections.rationale: The parties directly contest whether faith contributes a distinctive imperative toward goodness or merely attaches supernatural authority to moral capacities already available through reason and humanism.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Secular people can be equally good, but for vast numbers of believers faith actually supplies a distinctive imperative toward humility, forgiveness, compassion, and moral improvement.

sourceSpan.excerpt: they could easily have been inspired by humanism... But it was what led him to that... someone who is of no religious faith couldn't be just as good a person... religion can and does... give them an impulse to be better people.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: The golden-rule insight and moral argument arise from ordinary human reason and predate the cited religions, so divine command and religious dictatorship are unnecessary for knowing right from wrong.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The injunction not to do to another what would be repulsive done to yourself is found in the Analects of Confucius... We don't require divine permission to know right from wrong... We have the reasoning and the moral suasion of Socrates and of our own abilities.

lockedSections.title: Exclusivism, sectarian conflict, and reconciliation
lockedSections.rationale: This section preserves the debate's strongest concrete exchange over whether religion creates or intensifies division, or can instead furnish institutions and leaders capable of reconciliation.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Religious exclusivism is real but not essential to true religion; traditions of loving one's neighbor and examples such as cross-confessional Northern Ireland cooperation show faith can bridge divisions.

sourceSpan.excerpt: they can do and there are very many examples... Protestant Catholic churches got together... True religion is actually about embracing someone who is different... religion has tried to overcome those divides.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Rwanda, Northern Ireland, and the Middle East have tribal and political causes alongside religious ones, while religious actors have both harmed and protected people; these cases therefore do not justify condemning religion as a whole.

sourceSpan.excerpt: it really would be bizarre to say that the conflict in Rwanda was a result of the Catholic Church... members... stood up and protected and died alongside people... politics of the situation... not only religion.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: Monotheistic covenant and one-true-church claims turn faith into a force multiplier for ethnic and political division, making common humanism harder rather than easier.

sourceSpan.excerpt: an expression of exclusivism. This is our God... the one true church... faith is a fantastic force multiplier... of all things that are in fact divisive rather than inclusive.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: The fact that religious leaders later bridge conflict does not erase religion's role in producing or intensifying the divide, as illustrated by Northern Ireland and clerical participation in the Rwandan genocide.

sourceSpan.excerpt: where does the religious divide come from?... Rwanda... the Hutu power genocide... was preached from the pulpits... not entirely the fault of religion... it does tend to make it very very much worse.

lockedSections.title: Supernatural authority, freedom, and spiritual purpose
lockedSections.rationale: The closing exchange crystallizes the deepest route conflict: whether allegiance to transcendent authority disciplines human will toward good or exacts an unacceptable sacrifice of reason and autonomy.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Faith in a higher power need not produce servitude or certainty; it can acknowledge ignorance, coexist with science, discipline human will, and direct believers toward the best of humanity.

sourceSpan.excerpt: those who want to suppress freedom... are not confined to... religious faith... faith is not about certainty... awareness of my own ignorance... not... imprisoned by that superior will... discipline and use our own will.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: Even movements with heroic works are not worth the sacrifice of freedom demanded by infallible authority; religion similarly requires supernatural belief and submission to human interpreters claiming divine authority.

sourceSpan.excerpt: There was real heroism... but we opposed it... not worth the sacrifice of freedom... place yourself under an infallible leadership... religion means that you will have to follow someone... this person has divine authority.
